---
title: "Definitions"
subtitle: "The three faces of étale morphisms"
---
:::{ .callout-note title="Note"}
We will list some important equivalent definitions of étale morphisms and leave the discussion of their equivalence for later.
:::

## Equivalent definitions

:::{#def-étale name=""}
A morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ between schemes is **étale** if it is

1. locally of finite presentation,
2. flat, and
3. unramified.
:::

:::{#def-étale name=""}
A morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ between varieties over $k$ is **étale** if it induces isomorphisms on the tangent spaces at all points of $X$.
:::

:::{#def-étale name=""}
A morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ between schemes is **étale** if it is smooth of relative dimension $0$.
:::

::: {#rem-intuition name=""}
The second definition tells us that we can think of an étale map as a map that is locally an isomorphism. And for the definitions of the flat, unramified and smooth morphisms, see later.
:::

## Examples
:::{#exm-open-imm-is-etale name="open immersion"}
Every open immersion $U\hookrightarrow X$ is étale. Nothing changes near a point of $U$: we have only restricted our attention to a smaller open subset.
:::

:::{#exm-etale-cover-of-affine-line name=""}

Assume that $n$ is invertible in the base field. On the punctured affine
line, the map

$$
\mathbb G_m \longrightarrow \mathbb G_m, \qquad t\longmapsto t^n
$$

is étale. Infinitesimally, its derivative is $nt^{n-1}$, which never vanishes
on $\mathbb G_m$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the picture breaks"}
On the whole affine line, $t\mapsto t^n$ ramifies at $t=0$. The map is no
longer étale there: the branches collide.
:::
